description: Replace bits low through high, inclusively, of word with insert's bit pattern aligned so its bit zero lands at low. Preserve every bit outside that interval and return the resulting word.
constraints: Inputs and results are signed 32-bit integers. Interpret them as exactly 32 two's-complement bits, numbered 0 (least significant) through 31. Convert the resulting pattern back to its signed 32-bit value. Do not sign-extend into an unbounded Python integer or an extra JavaScript bit.

0 <= low <= high <= 31. The unsigned 32-bit interpretation of insert fits within high-low+1 bits. Negative insert values are therefore valid only for a full-width interval. Inputs satisfy these preconditions; invalid bounds are not a request to return zero.
Do not mutate inputs. The full-width interval [0,31] is valid and returns insert.
why: OR alone cannot replace an existing one with zero. First clear exactly the destination interval, then OR the aligned replacement into that cleared region. A width-sized mask describes the replacement independently of its destination.
correctness: The mask has ones exactly at the interval positions. AND with its complement keeps every outside bit and clears every inside bit. The fitting insertion has no bits beyond that interval after shifting. OR therefore sets each inside bit to the corresponding insertion bit and cannot affect an outside bit. The signed conversion changes only the numerical interpretation, not the 32-bit pattern.
walkthrough: For word 240 (binary 11110000), insert 5 (101), low 1 and high 3, clearing positions 1..3 leaves 11110000. Aligning 101 yields 00001010. OR produces 11111010, or 250. Inserting zero into those positions would clear them rather than preserving old ones.
time: O(1) time for a fixed 32-bit word: a constant number of masks, shifts and bitwise operations.
edges: Full-width replacement, including a negative insertion.
A one-bit interval at position zero or 31.
Zero insertion clears old one bits; unrelated bits remain set.
related: swap_bits changes only two positions and is not this inclusive-range replacement.
title: Insertion

csharp.signature: int InsertBits(int word, int insert, int low, int high)

python.signature: def InsertBits(word: int, insert: int, low: int, high: int) -> int
python.starterCode:
def InsertBits(word: int, insert: int, low: int, high: int) -> int:
    return 0
python.solutionCode:
def InsertBits(word: int, insert: int, low: int, high: int) -> int:
    width = high - low + 1
    mask = (1 << width) - 1
    bits = ((word & 0xFFFFFFFF) & ~(mask << low)) | ((insert & mask) << low)
    return bits if bits < 0x80000000 else bits - 0x100000000

description: Return the exact terminating binary fraction for number, beginning with a binary point and no leading zero, or the literal string ERROR if the input is outside (0,1) or needs more than 31 fractional bits. Stop after the last one; do not append trailing zeros, round or truncate.
constraints: number is a finite IEEE-754 binary64 value. Convert that actual value, not an imagined exact rational inferred from its decimal spelling. For example the binary64 value written 0.1 needs more than the allowed bits and returns ERROR.

The output limit is 32 characters INCLUDING the initial point, hence at most 31 fractional bits. This bank uses the strict boundary of the public second implementation; the two public implementations disagree by one at that boundary. A representation requiring 32 fractional bits must fail.
0.5 returns .1; zero, one, negative values and values above one return ERROR. Preserve the input.
why: Multiplying a binary fraction by two moves its next digit to the units position. Emit that zero or one and remove it, leaving exactly the still-unrepresented suffix. A zero suffix proves the representation is complete; a nonzero suffix after 31 digits proves that returning the accumulated prefix would truncate it.
correctness: After emitting k digits, the original value equals their fractional value plus the current remainder divided by 2^k. Doubling and subtracting the emitted units digit preserves this invariant, with remainder in [0,1). These operations are exact for the admitted binary64 values: doubling shifts the exponent, and subtracting one from a value in [1,2) loses no fractional information. Zero remainder gives the exact value with no trailing zeros. If the remainder is nonzero after 31 steps, at least another digit is necessary, so ERROR is required.
walkthrough: For 0.625, doubling yields 1.25: emit 1 and keep .25. Doubling .25 yields .5: emit 0. Doubling .5 yields 1: emit 1 and the remainder is zero. The result is .101. The value 2^-31 yields a point, 30 zeros and one; 2^-32 exceeds this bank's 32-character limit.
time: O(b) time for b emitted fractional digits, with b <= 31. The fixed limit makes worst-case time O(1); no unbounded search for termination occurs.
space: O(b) output/builder space, bounded by 32 characters.
edges: Exact powers of two at the final accepted and first rejected bit positions.
A nonterminating-within-limit binary64 fraction such as 0.1.
Zero, one and other finite out-of-range values.
related: String-based decimal-to-base conversion does not define the same binary64 input or exact-output limit.
title: Binary to String

description: Return the largest length of a consecutive run of one bits obtainable by changing at most one zero bit to one in word's fixed 32-bit representation. The run cannot extend outside positions 0..31. If all 32 bits are already one, return 32.
constraints: Inputs and results are signed 32-bit integers. Interpret them as exactly 32 two's-complement bits, numbered 0 (least significant) through 31. Convert the resulting pattern back to its signed 32-bit value. Do not sign-extend into an unbounded Python integer or an extra JavaScript bit.
All signed 32-bit inputs are valid. Leading zero bits are part of the word, so zero can become a run of length one. No flip is required when it cannot improve the run. Preserve the input.
why: A bit interval can become all ones with at most one flip exactly when it contains at most one zero. Maintaining the longest valid window ending at each bit therefore examines every candidate without constructing 32 modified words.
correctness: Before recording each window length, remove leftmost bits until the window contains at most one zero. Its left boundary is the earliest boundary that makes this window valid: an earlier discarded boundary would retain two zeros. Thus it is the longest valid interval ending at that right boundary. Every obtainable run is such a valid interval and has some right endpoint, so taking the maximum over all 32 endpoints gives exactly the best run. Negative numbers are read through their fixed 32-bit patterns, with logical bit extraction.
walkthrough: The low pattern 11011101111 contains two zeros separating runs of lengths 2,3,4. Flipping the zero between the final runs joins 3+1+4=8 ones. Joining the first two gives only 6. The sliding window discards enough of the first run when the second zero arrives, rather than allowing both zeros to be flipped.
time: O(w) time for word width w=32: each boundary advances at most w times, hence O(1) in this fixed-width domain.
space: O(1) auxiliary space for two boundaries, zero count and maximum.
edges: Zero gives one; minus one gives 32.
Two adjacent zeros cannot both be flipped.
The sign bit and runs touching either word boundary.
related: A longest-one substring problem on arbitrary text does not include the fixed signed-word conversion rules.
title: Flip Bit to Win

description: Return [smaller,larger], the nearest strictly smaller and strictly larger positive signed 32-bit integers having the same number of set bits as number. Use -1 independently for a side with no such integer. Do not wrap into the sign bit or include zero as a positive neighbor.
constraints: 1 <= number <= 2147483647. Search only the positive 31-bit range 1..2147483647. A result has exactly two entries, smaller first. Preserve the input.
For 1 return [-1,2]. For 2147483647 return [-1,-1], because there is no other positive 31-bit word with 31 set bits.
why: Adding the lowest set bit carries the lowest movable run of ones into its next zero position. To get the smallest larger word with the same weight, put all remaining ones into the lowest available positions. Complementing within 31 bits reverses numeric order, so the same successor operation on the complement yields the predecessor without another complicated bit-case algorithm.
correctness: For a nonzero value, let its lowest run of ones have r bits after z trailing zeros. Adding its lowest set bit moves that run into the first zero above it. Changing a higher position would produce a larger candidate, while no smaller-position change can increase the number with the same weight. The XOR/divide/shift expression reconstructs exactly r-1 low ones below the moved bit, giving the minimum possible suffix. Reject a carried value beyond the positive 31-bit maximum. For the smaller neighbor, complementation maps k set bits to 31-k and reverses order; the least greater valid complement therefore maps back to the greatest smaller original. A zero complement has no same-weight greater word.
walkthrough: For 12 (01100), its lowest set bit is 4. Adding it gives 10000; the two original ones require one remaining low one, producing 10001, or 17, as the nearest larger value. The nearest smaller value is 01010, or 10. The result is [10,17]; closest absolute distance alone would not answer both requested sides.
time: O(1) word operations in the fixed 31-bit domain, including two successor computations; there is no scan across integer values.
space: O(1) auxiliary space plus the two-entry result.
edges: A single set bit at either end of the permitted range.
All low bits one, no smaller neighbor, or no larger neighbor.
Long runs of trailing zeros/ones and the signed maximum.
related: closest_int_same_weight minimizes distance to one result and is not an exact duplicate of returning both ordered neighbors.
title: Next Number

description: Return the minimum number of individual bit flips needed to turn first's 32-bit representation into second's. A flip changes one chosen zero to one or one to zero; no other operation is available.
constraints: Inputs and results are signed 32-bit integers. Interpret them as exactly 32 two's-complement bits, numbered 0 (least significant) through 31. Convert the resulting pattern back to its signed 32-bit value. Do not sign-extend into an unbounded Python integer or an extra JavaScript bit.
All signed 32-bit input values are valid. The result is an integer from 0 through 32. Preserve inputs.
why: A differing position must be flipped at least once, while an equal position needs no flip. XOR marks exactly the differing positions, so counting its set bits attains that lower bound. Clearing its lowest set bit counts one difference per iteration without scanning equal positions.
correctness: Each XOR bit is one exactly when the two input bits differ. Every such position needs a flip, and flipping exactly those positions transforms the first word into the second. For a nonzero pattern d, d AND (d-1) clears exactly its lowest set bit and leaves every higher set bit unchanged. Thus the loop performs one iteration per required flip and stops after counting them all.
walkthrough: For 29 (11101) and 15 (01111), XOR is 10010. Clearing the lowest one changes it to 10000; clearing again yields zero. Two flips suffice and both differing positions necessarily need a flip.
time: O(k) bit operations for k differing bits, with k <= 32; O(1) for the fixed 32-bit domain. The loop clears a set bit rather than shifting through all positions.
edges: Equal inputs require zero flips.
Zero and -1 differ at all 32 positions.
The sign bit alone differs between 0 and the minimum signed integer.
related: A population-count helper may be reused only after establishing the 32-bit XOR domain; unbounded signed popcount is not equivalent.
title: Conversion

python.signature: def CountBitChanges(first: int, second: int) -> int
python.starterCode:
def CountBitChanges(first: int, second: int) -> int:
    return 0
python.solutionCode:
def CountBitChanges(first: int, second: int) -> int:
    difference = (first ^ second) & 0xFFFFFFFF
    count = 0
    while difference:
        difference &= difference - 1
        count += 1
    return count

description: Swap every adjacent pair of bits in word's fixed 32-bit representation: positions (0,1), (2,3), and so on through (30,31). Return the signed integer represented by the resulting bits.
constraints: Inputs and results are signed 32-bit integers. Interpret them as exactly 32 two's-complement bits, numbered 0 (least significant) through 31. Convert the resulting pattern back to its signed 32-bit value. Do not sign-extend into an unbounded Python integer or an extra JavaScript bit.
All signed 32-bit input values are valid. All sixteen pairs are swapped simultaneously; there is no pair-selection argument. Preserve the input.
why: The even-position mask selects one member of every pair, and the odd-position mask selects the other. Shift the even bits left and the odd bits logically right, then combine them. Separating the groups prevents a moved bit from being moved again.
correctness: Every original even-position bit moves exactly one place left into its paired odd position; every original odd-position bit moves exactly one place right into its paired even position. The masks partition all 32 positions, and their destinations are disjoint, so OR combines exactly one source for each destination. Logical shifting avoids introducing new leading ones. No position crosses between different pairs.
walkthrough: The low byte 01100101 (101) has pairs 01,10,01,01 when read from its high end. Swapping within each pair gives 10011010 (154). Applying the operation again returns 01100101. A top-bit move may make the signed result negative without changing the bit rule.
time: O(1) time for fixed-width masks, two shifts and one OR.
edges: Zero and all ones are unchanged.
A one at position 31 moves to 30 without sign extension.
Alternating masks swap with one another; applying twice restores the original.
related: swap_bits accepts two selected positions; this exercise swaps all sixteen pairs.
title: Pairwise Swap

python.solutionCode:
def SwapAdjacentBits(word: int) -> int:
    bits = word & 0xFFFFFFFF
    result = ((bits & 0x55555555) << 1) | ((bits & 0xAAAAAAAA) >> 1)
    return result if result < 0x80000000 else result - 0x100000000

description: Set to one every pixel from x1 through x2 inclusively on row y of a byte-packed monochrome screen. Mutate the supplied byte buffer in place, preserve its length, and preserve every other pixel. Existing ones stay set; this operation draws onto the screen rather than replacing its row.
constraints: width is in pixels, is divisible by eight and lies in 8..4096. Height is 1..256 and screen contains exactly (width/8)*height bytes. Coordinates satisfy 0 <= x1 <= x2 < width and 0 <= y < height. Inputs meet these shape/range preconditions.
Rows are stored top-to-bottom, bytes left-to-right. Within a byte, its most significant bit is the leftmost pixel. Pixel (x,y) uses byte y*(width/8)+floor(x/8) and bit 7-(x mod 8).

The callable receives byte[] in C#/Java, Uint8Array in JavaScript, bytearray in Python, or vector<uint8_t>& in C++. Examples encode bytes as integers 0..255, including Java bytes whose signed display would otherwise be negative. Return void; the displayed result is the original mutated buffer. Do not resize, replace or reorder the buffer.
why: Whole interior bytes correspond to eight pixels to set, while only the first and last bytes need partial masks. Intersecting the start and end masks also handles a line contained in one byte. OR preserves every preexisting one outside and inside the line.
correctness: For each affected byte, the start bound is x1 mod 8 only at the first byte and zero otherwise; the end bound is x2 mod 8 only at the last byte and seven otherwise. The two masks have ones from the start rightward and from the end leftward. Their intersection therefore selects exactly the line pixels within that byte, including when both endpoints share it. OR sets these bits without clearing any original bit. Only bytes on row y between the endpoint bytes are written, so all other pixels and buffer length remain unchanged.
walkthrough: On a two-byte row initially [128,1], draw x=3 through x=10. The first-byte mask is 00011111 and the last-byte mask is 11100000. OR gives [159,225]. The old pixel at x=0 and the old pixel at x=15 remain set. A line x=3..5 in one byte uses the intersection 00011100, not the union of the two partial masks.
time: O(1+floor(x2/8)-floor(x1/8)) time, one write per affected byte; independent of the rest of the screen size.
space: O(1) auxiliary space. The judge display copies the final buffer for reporting, which is not storage used by the submitted algorithm.
edges: One pixel and both endpoints in a single byte.
Exact whole-byte endpoints and partial edges across multiple bytes.
Nonzero initial screen, repeated drawing, first/last rows and pixels.
related: A matrix fill or text rendering task does not share this packed-byte layout and mutation contract.
title: Draw Line

csharp.signature: void DrawHorizontalLine(byte[] screen, int width, int x1, int x2, int y)

javascript.signature: function DrawHorizontalLine(screen, width, x1, x2, y)

python.signature: def DrawHorizontalLine(screen: bytearray, width: int, x1: int, x2: int, y: int) -> None
python.starterCode:
def DrawHorizontalLine(screen: bytearray, width: int, x1: int, x2: int, y: int) -> None:
    pass
python.solutionCode:
def DrawHorizontalLine(screen: bytearray, width: int, x1: int, x2: int, y: int) -> None:
    first, last = x1 // 8, x2 // 8
    row = y * (width // 8)
    for byte in range(first, last + 1):
        start = x1 % 8 if byte == first else 0
        end = x2 % 8 if byte == last else 7
        mask = (255 >> start) & ((255 << (7 - end)) & 255)
        screen[row + byte] |= mask
